newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada not seen benefiting from US/EU genetics row.
newsitem.headline: Canada not seen benefiting from US/EU genetics row.

text.p: Canada's exports of canola and canola oil are not likely to rise in response to European concerns about a new variety of genetically altered U.S. soybeans, Canola Council of Canada vice president Tony Zatylny said.

"We do not benefit from this flap, although we are watching very carefully to see what this means for our canola exports in the long term," Zatylny told Reuters, noting that a percentage of Canadian canola is produced from transgenic seed.
EuroCommerce, a trade group that represents food retailers and wholesalers in 20 European countries, said on Thursday that it wanted gene-altered soybeans to be identified in foodstuffs.

U.S. farmers are just starting this year's soybean harvest, which included the first batches of a genetically altered soybean strain developed by U.S. chemical company Monsanto to withstand its herbicide, Roundup.

The American Soybean Association estimates that only 30-50 million bushels of "Roundup Ready" genetically altered soybeans will be produced this year, or at most about two percent of the estimated 2.3 billion bushel U.S. crop.
A report from Germany's farm price office ZMP on Thursday said rapeseed oil was replacing soyoil in some European buying now because of doubts about consumer acceptance and trade rules.

Europe was still a relatively small market for Canadian canola, which mainly goes to Japan, the U.S. and Mexico. From 1989 to 1995 Canada exported about 380,000 tonnes of canola to Europe annually, against 1.7 million tonnes to Japan, he said.
Zatylny said five herbicide-tolerant transgenic varieties of canola were registered in Canada, representing three to four percent of nine million acres of canola planted this year.
Canada already has a system in place to identify genetically altered canola, he said.
Canadian canola exports to Japan were identity-preserved and marked transgenic and non-transgenic, Zatylny said.
"However, it appears that we will soon have clearance to export transgenic canola to Japan, probably next year," Zatylny said.
But he said the genetics question has to be cleared up in Europe, which does not have all the rules in place for accepting genetically altered crops.
"Now the question is, if they (EU) approve genetically altered soybeans, will that approval extend to canola?" he said.
